Capital One.

Terms of fly.
Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Today is Black Friday, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season, but higher
everyday costs are putting the pressure on consumers this year.
NPR's Alina Seljuk reports.
All the surveys seem to find people saying they might have to cut back on other spending
in order to spend during the holiday season.
That's especially true the lower you go along the income brackets.
At the National Retail Federation, their chief economist, Mark Matthews, was saying that people
have been feeling pretty strongly about prioritizing their holiday spending.
There's almost a moat around that form of spending.
They care about spending on their family and they're choosing to do that rather than go
for a meal out or maybe they'll travel a little bit less.
Right now, the biggest drivers of inflation are gas prices and housing costs, to some
extent groceries, so goods, all this stuff like gifts, they have not been rising in price
as dramatically.
That's NPR's Alina Seljuk reporting.
Senate Democrats are set to hold leadership elections next week where the race for majority
leader is contested.
NPR's Alina Moore reports lawmakers are deciding between Chuck Schumer of New York and Chris
Van Hollen of Maryland.
Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change in Washington when they retake a majority
next year, but they're split over who should lead that shift.
Schumer, who's been the top Democrat in the Senate since 2017, says he has enough votes
to win.
Van Hollen calls himself an underdog and says he's running on more of a populist message,
hoping to capitalize on broader dissatisfaction voters have with the party establishment.
However, unlike the midterms, this isn't an election decided by voters.
It'll come down to other senators from their own party and will be decided by secret ballot.
Alina Moore, NPR News.
Democrats in Spain are holding their final rallies tonight ahead of Sunday's national
election.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is fighting to stay in office, but polls suggest
conservatives could win a majority with the far-right Vox Party.
NPR's Miguel Macias reports from Seville.
On the last day of campaigning, everything is on the line, and the outcome of Sunday's
election is anyone's guess.
That's why candidates for the main parties are holding multiple events.
Saturday is what's known as the day of reflection.
Candidates are not allowed to ask for people's votes.
The campaign has been marked by polarization.
None of the two main parties, the socialists with Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and the
conservative party, Partido Popular, with Alberto Núñez Fijo, are expected to be able
to govern on their own.
That's why in this election, far-right and far-left parties are key, as they will likely
play kingmakers after results are in.
Miguel Macias, NPR News, Seville, Spain.
This is NPR News.
The Environmental Protection Agency says test results could come in today from samples collected
following Wednesday's controlled explosion of a stockpile of hazardous chemicals in southeast
Iowa.
The EPA took more than 1,500 samples of air, water, soil and dust before the blast and
more than 1,000 more afterward.
So far, the agency has not reported finding lead in the air since the blast.
The Army says the stockpile of lead azide was deteriorating and could have exploded
on its own as temperatures dropped.
Major League Baseball is approaching an expected lockout.
NPR's John Stolenes reports the current labor agreement between the Owners and Players
Union expires on Tuesday.
Owners want to establish a salary cap and floor for players.
They say a cap would allow smaller market teams like the world champion brewers to better
compete with big spending teams like the Dodgers and Mets.
Major League Baseball Commissioner Rob Manfred says he believes most fans want this too.
They want a salary cap and floor and on that we will not compromise.
But the Players Union disagrees and is adamant that any new agreement cannot include a cap
on players' salaries.
As the two sides dig in, there are worries this lockout could extend into the regular
season in March.
The last time games were lost due to a labor dispute was following the players' strike
of 1994 and 95.
John Stolenes, NPR News.
On Wall Street, Dow futures are up 647 points before the open.
This is NPR News.
